newsitem.title: USA: Food Lion judge considers damages.
newsitem.headline: Food Lion judge considers damages.

text.p: A judge hearing pre-trial motions in a lawsuit by grocery chain Food Lion Inc against the ABC television network was considering whether or not Food Lion would be able to claim any damages.
Food Lion filed a lawsuit against ABC in 1992 over the network's "PrimeTime Live" show that November claiming that Food Lion handled meat and fish in an unsanitary and deceptive way.
Food Lion, which operates largely in the Southeast, was charging "fraud, deceptive trade practices, conpiracy and breach of duty of loyalty" against ABC and four producers.
Food Lion was reportedly seeking as much as $2.5 billion, but spokeswoman Chris Ahearn would not confirm the amount.
"We don't have a solid number," Ahearn said. "What we're waiting for is the judge to determine the kinds of damages that Food Lion can seek.
Damages can range from as much as Food Lion says it lost after the show aired to the costs Food Lion incurred to train the producers who worked undercover at two of its stores, according to analysts.
The trial was due to begin on December 9, in a federal court in Greensboro, North Carolina and last about five weeks.

A lawyer for ABC said during pretrial hearings that the network cannot be ordered to pay damages for airing the investigative piece. A free press needs breathing space and deception was an acceptable ethical technique when used by media to collect information, he said.
But Food Lion countered that ABC violated ethics when its producers staged events to sell tainted merchandise.
Pretrial hearings were expected to end this week.
"We expect (the judge's decision on damages) on Friday and then we can calculate a realistic figure that we can argue before a jury," Ahearn said.

The legal battle between Salisbury, N.C.-based Food Lion, a unit of Belgian retailer Ets Delhaize Freres et Cie "LE LION" SA, and New York-based ABC, a unit of Walt Disney Co, centers on unaired videotape showing ABC producers pushed Food Lion workers to sell out-of-date merchandise and changed expiration dates on other merchandise.
"(The unaired tapes) go directly to fraud and fiduciary duties. The out takes show examples of staging by the producers...," said Ahearn.
Ahearn said the truth or falsity of the broadcast was not being decided, but whether or not ABC broke the law when it provided Food Lion with false job applications and false references.

"As paid employees, we expected the employees to fulfill their jobs, but instead they staged news and worked for ABC and not food lion," she added. The chain's sales plummeted after the broadcast, but analysts cautioned stores in Texas were struggling then. Ken Gassman of Davenport & Co said the show "appeared to be the catalyst" for a slide in earnings from the 1992 fourth quarter through 1994 and part of 1995.

"It has just been this year that earnings have gotten back on the trend line," Gassman said. "They were going up four or five pennies per share each year. So it took them about three years to get back on trend after the PrimeTime Live program."
Food Lion's earnings last year were $0.36 per share. But this year the grocer was due to earn $0.45 a share, according to analysts' estimates compiled by I/B/E/S.
He said same-store sales had negative comparisons for four straight quarters during the period also.
"The only time in a 10-year period that the company's same store sales were negative was immediately following the PrimeTime Live airing," he added.
